note: The County of Toulouse — the dominant power in Languedoc — was drawn into the French orbit through the Albigensian Crusade (1209–1229). Count Raymond VI of Toulouse, suspected of harboring Cathars, was excommunicated and his lands attacked. The Treaty of Paris (1229) forced Count Raymond VII to surrender half his lands, to hunt heretics, and to marry his daughter Jeanne to Alphonse of Poitiers (Louis IX's brother). When Alphonse and Jeanne died without children (1271), Toulouse reverted to the French crown, completing the absorption of Languedoc and permanently eliminating the distinct Occitanian cultural sphere.

_quarry.structural_significance: The Albigensian Crusade converts what would have been a gradual political absorption into a cultural catastrophe; Toulouse's absorption eliminates the most sophisticated secular courtly culture in 12th-century Europe (the troubadour tradition); the Inquisition established in Toulouse becomes a model for later inquisitorial institutions
